generatedProse.concept-context: Across the School of Sport, presentations are a familiar form of assessment. Whatever your subject, you might present a study you have read, a piece of your own analysis, or a poster at a conference-style session. A sport and exercise science student might talk through lab findings, while a coaching student presents a session review and a management student pitches a participation plan. The methods differ, but the point is shared: you communicate an argument or set of findings clearly to an audience, usually with slides. A sport presentation develops the academic voice the school values, and the clear communication that research, coaching and professional practice all demand.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two sport and exercise science students given the same brief: a ten-minute presentation on a physiology study from their module.

Tom treats the task as reading out information. He copies his notes onto slides and plans to read them aloud, line by line, covering the method and the VO2 max results. The study is described, but the audience is left reading dense slides while Tom reads too. His presentation is really a lab report read out, not a talk. This misses what a presentation is for.

Amara treats the task as communicating a point to an audience. She works out one clear message about what the study shows about aerobic fitness, chooses what the audience needs to hear, and uses her slides to support the spoken argument rather than carry it. Her talk has a shape and a purpose. This is what an academic presentation is: a spoken argument, made clearly to listeners.

Both had the same brief. Only Amara understood that a presentation is communication to an audience, not a document read aloud.
generatedProse.summary: An academic presentation in the School of Sport is a spoken piece of assessed work in which you communicate an argument or findings to an audience, usually with slides. It develops your academic voice and builds transferable skills such as clear communication. You can now explain what a presentation is, give an example of a skill it builds, and recognise the main types used for assessment. The next lessons turn this into practice: how you plan and structure a presentation, and how you design its visual aids.

check.body: In the worked example, what did Amara understand that Tom did not?

items.text: That a presentation is communication to an audience, not a document read aloud.
That more slides always make a presentation better.
That the study should be described as quickly as possible.
That reading notes aloud word for word is the safest approach.

feedback.correct: That's right. Amara understood a presentation is communication to an audience.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara grasped about the purpose of a presentation.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara understood a presentation is communication to an audience, not a document read aloud. The other options mistake slides, speed or reciting for the point.
